unit.title: Harness Engineering Fundamentals
unit.moc: agent = model + harness — the 8 components — harness beats model — failure stats — tribunal's map — sensors proven

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint 2 — gate
checkpoint.prompt: Classify a fictional system against the 8 harness components and say which layer the tribunal itself was weakest in.

facts.text: An agent is two parts: the **model** that reasons, and the **harness**, everything wrapped around it - what the model sees, what it can do, how it recovers.
Harness engineering is its own discipline, distinct from prompt engineering and model selection. Keep the model fixed and behavior still changes completely when the wrapper changes.
Same model, different harness: swap the guides and sensors and the engine starts catching errors it used to ship. Same brain, different agent.
Saying 'the model is the agent' misses half the machine: the model is one component among many. In the learn path, the checkpoint gating this unit is the verification layer turned into a quiz.

options: everything around the model — what it sees, what it can do, how it recovers

exercises.prompt: Harness engineering is the same thing as model selection.

facts.text: A standard harness inventories into eight components: guides, sensors, memory/state, tool-execution, guardrails, loop controller, verification, and failure handler. Each owns one job in the agent's life cycle.
Guides are the feedforward layer: `AGENTS.md` and conventions shape behavior before the model acts. Sensors are the feedback layer: linters, type checks, and LLM-as-judge report how it did.
Guardrails encode policy the model cannot overrule. The tribunal's own examples are structural rules like `DeepSeek-once` and `MAX_LANES=4`.
Verification is the most-skipped layer: a sensor that only confirms output is non-empty passes trivially. Real verification proves the thing actually works.
The inventory is hands-on here: the complete exercise below fills in memory/state and verification, and the unit checkpoint maps a fictional system onto all eight components.

exercises.prompt: Match each component to its role.
Which component is the FEEDFORWARD layer?
The 8 components: guides, sensors, ___, tool-execution, guardrails, loop controller, ___, failure handler.

facts.text: Improving the harness beats swapping the model: better guides, sensors, guardrails, and loops make the same engine markedly more capable.
The cited evidence: harness changes delivered 5 to 14 benchmark points and -20% tokens while the model stayed the same. The gain came from the wrapper, not a bigger brain.
Manus rewrote its harness five times in six months on one unchanged model - treating the harness as the product.
The tempting move is 'just buy a bigger model'. The literature argues the opposite: invest in the layers around whichever model you already run.

options: 5–14 benchmark points and −20% tokens on the same model

exercises.prompt: Manus rewrote its harness ___ in 6 months with the same model.
The moral of this lesson is:
options: improve the harness around the model

facts.text: The base rate is brutal: about 88% of agent projects never reach production. Building a demo is easy; operating reliably is the hard part.
About 27% of failures trace to data quality: the agent reasons over bad or unverified inputs, so even a perfect model produces wrong answers.
Weak verification is the most-skipped layer: models say done when they're not done, and a sensor that only checks for non-empty output passes trivially.
These numbers are not an argument for a bigger model. They are an argument for the layers teams skip: verification and data quality.

exercises.prompt: About what share of agent projects never reach production?

facts.text: Mapped against the eight components, the tribunal splits cleanly: strong in memory/state and guardrails, weak in sensors, and verification held as doctrine rather than machinery.
Memory/state is strong because it is files-only with a proven clean-session bootstrap: nothing depends on a hidden service remembering state between runs.
Guardrails are strong because they are structural: `DeepSeek-once` and `MAX_LANES=4` bind every lane no matter what any model prefers.
Sensors are weak because they lean on byte counts - the 'trivial check' the literature warns about. Size confirmed is not correctness proven.
Verification is 'doctrine, not machinery': the habit of challenging and citing stands in for an automated gate. The unit checkpoint asks you to name this weakest layer yourself.

exercises.prompt: Which layers of the tribunal are STRONGEST?
The tribunal's sensors are weak because:
options: byte count is the “trivial check” the literature warns about
there are too many of them
they run on the wrong lane

exercises.prompt: The tribunal's verification was described as:

facts.text: The sensor gap from the statistics is not theoretical: two live defects slipped through the hub's shallow checks.
Defect 1: `class: lane-benchmark` auto-picked 5 lanes, blowing past `MAX_LANES=4` and violating the `DeepSeek-once` guard. No sensor checked the lane count against the guardrail.
Defect 2: `hub verdict` matched slugs by substring, so a slug contained inside another silently rewrote the wrong ledger row. An exact-match sensor would have caught it.
Neither bug is cosmetic: both are exactly the shallow-sensor pattern the failure statistics warned about, caught live inside the tribunal's own harness.

options: 5 lanes were auto-picked, failing MAX_LANES=4 and DeepSeek-once
substring match could rewrite the wrong ledger row

exercises.prompt: Why do these matter as a lesson?
options: both are exactly the sensor gap they prove
